## Part 1 — Setup & Load (15%)

Load `retail_sales.csv` into a tibble called `sales`.

```{r}
#| message: false
# TODO 1a: load tidyverse and read retail_sales.csv into `sales`
library(tidyverse)

sales <- read_csv("retail_sales.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(sales)
```

Report, using inline code (not just printed in the chunk above): how many
rows and columns does the raw data have?

The raw dataset has `r nrow(sales)` rows and `r ncol(sales)` columns.

## Part 2 — Clean (20%)

**2a.** Report how many missing values exist in `units_sold` and `revenue`.

```{r}
# TODO 2a
sales |>
  summarise(
    missing_units_sold = sum(is.na(units_sold)),
    missing_revenue    = sum(is.na(revenue))
  )
```

**2b.** Clean the data: remove exact duplicate rows, fill missing
`units_sold`/`revenue` with their column medians, and standardize the
`category` column into a new column with **exactly 5** distinct values
(lowercase, trimmed, with underscores/extra spaces collapsed to a single
space, and the `"cloth ing"` typo explicitly corrected to `"clothing"`).
Save the result as `sales_clean`.

```{r}
# TODO 2b
sales_clean <- sales |>
  # 1. remove exact duplicate rows
  distinct() |>
  # 2. fill missing values with column medians
  mutate(
    units_sold = if_else(is.na(units_sold),
                         median(units_sold, na.rm = TRUE), units_sold),
    revenue    = if_else(is.na(revenue),
                         median(revenue, na.rm = TRUE), revenue)
  ) |>
  # 3. standardize category into a new column
  mutate(
    category_clean = category |>
      str_to_lower() |>
      str_replace_all("_", " ") |>
      str_squish() |>
      str_replace("^cloth ing$", "clothing")
  )

# check: no missing values left, and exactly 5 categories
colSums(is.na(sales_clean))
count(sales_clean, category_clean)
```

Report, using inline code: how many rows remain after removing
duplicates, and how many distinct categories does `sales_clean` have?

After cleaning, the dataset has `r nrow(sales_clean)` rows and
`r n_distinct(sales_clean$category_clean)` distinct categories.

## Part 3 — Analyze (25%)

**3a.** Compute total revenue per `store`, sorted highest to lowest.

```{r}
# TODO 3a
store_revenue <- sales_clean |>
  group_by(store) |>
  summarise(total_revenue = sum(revenue)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_revenue))

store_revenue
```

**3b.** Compute total revenue per `category`, sorted highest to lowest.

```{r}
# TODO 3b
category_revenue <- sales_clean |>
  group_by(category_clean) |>
  summarise(total_revenue = sum(revenue)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_revenue))

category_revenue
```

Report, using inline code: which store and which category had the
highest total revenue?

The highest-revenue store was `r store_revenue$store[1]`, and the
highest-revenue category was `r category_revenue$category_clean[1]`.

## Part 4 — Visualize (20%)

**4a.** Create a bar chart of total revenue by category, with a title and
axis labels.

```{r}
# TODO 4a
ggplot(category_revenue,
       aes(x = reorder(category_clean, -total_revenue), y = total_revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Revenue by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Total Revenue (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4b.** Create a box plot of revenue by category. Use `#| echo: false` on
this chunk so only the chart appears in your rendered report, not the
code.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# TODO 4b
ggplot(sales_clean, aes(x = category_clean, y = revenue)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Revenue per Transaction by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Revenue (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Part 5 — Written Reflection & AI Disclosure (20%)

**5a.** Why does writing this analysis as a Quarto report, instead of a
plain R script, change how much you (or someone else) can trust the
numbers in Part 3? Answer in 2–3 sentences.

In a Quarto report, the code, its output, and the written conclusions are
produced together in one render from the raw `retail_sales.csv`, so every
number in Part 3 (and every inline value in the text) is recomputed
directly from the data rather than copied by hand. If the data or a
cleaning step changes, re-rendering updates all results automatically, and
anyone can re-run the same file to verify them. With a plain script, the
numbers in a write-up can drift out of sync with the code, and a reader has
no guarantee the reported results came from that exact code.
